title: Andromeda
subtitle: The Princess

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: November (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object
facts.value: M31, the Andromeda Galaxy: spiral galaxy, 2.5 million light-years, magnitude 3.1

essay:
Andromeda is one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy in the second century. In Greek myth she was the daughter of Cepheus and Cassiopeia, chained to a rock as an offering to the sea monster Cetus and rescued by Perseus. All of those figures lie next to her in the sky.

The constellation is a chain of stars running north-east from the corner of the Square of Pegasus. That corner star, Alpheratz (magnitude 2.06), belongs to Andromeda, although older charts counted it in both figures. Mirach, at 2.05, is fractionally brighter and is formally the brightest star. Almach, the third bright star along the chain, is a double star that shows gold and blue components in a small telescope.

The best-known object here is the Andromeda Galaxy, M31, a spiral galaxy about 2.5 million light-years away and the nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way. At magnitude 3.1 it is visible to the naked eye from a dark site as an elongated haze. To find it, start at Mirach, step north-west to the fainter star Mu Andromedae, and continue about the same distance again. Andromeda is best placed in the evening in November and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 36° S.

title: Antlia
subtitle: The Air Pump

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: April (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Antlia was introduced by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille, who mapped the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope in 1751 and 1752 and published his new constellations in the 1750s. He named it la Machine Pneumatique, the air pump, and the Latin name was later shortened to Antlia. Like most of Lacaille's figures, it commemorates a scientific instrument rather than a figure from myth.

It is a small, faint area with no star brighter than fourth magnitude. The brightest, Alpha Antliae, is an orange giant of magnitude 4.25 with no traditional name. The constellation lies south of the long body of Hydra, between Alphard and the stars of Vela. The easiest way to locate it is to identify those neighbours first and then look in the sparse gap between them.

Antlia lies well south of the celestial equator. From the Southern Hemisphere it climbs high in the evening around April; from mid-northern latitudes it stays low in the south, and it is fully visible only from south of about 49° N. Its deep-sky objects are faint galaxies, including members of the Antlia Cluster, which need a telescope of moderate size.

title: Apus
subtitle: The Bird of Paradise

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: July (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Apus is one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius from observations made by the Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman on voyages to the East Indies in the 1590s. It first appeared on a celestial globe in 1598 and was included in Johann Bayer's atlas Uranometria in 1603. The name refers to the bird of paradise, which European traders knew from skins brought back from New Guinea. The Greek word apous means "without feet", because the skins were often prepared with the feet removed.

The constellation lies close to the south celestial pole, between Triangulum Australe and Octans. Its stars are faint: the brightest, Alpha Apodis, is an orange giant of magnitude 3.80. Find Apus by locating the three bright stars of Triangulum Australe and looking a little further toward the pole.

From southern temperate latitudes Apus is circumpolar and can be seen on any clear night, but it stands highest in the evening around July. It is fully visible only from south of about 6° N, so it is out of reach for most northern observers. It contains a few faint globular clusters, such as NGC 6101, that need a telescope.

title: Aquarius
subtitle: The Water Bearer

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: October (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object
facts.value: Helix Nebula (NGC 7293, Caldwell 63): planetary nebula, 650 light-years, magnitude 7.3

essay:
Aquarius is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations and one of the oldest recorded figures, with roots in Babylonian star lore, where it was a figure pouring water. Greek writers identified the water bearer with Ganymede, the youth carried to Olympus to serve as cupbearer to the gods. It is a zodiac constellation, so the Sun, Moon and planets pass through it.

Aquarius is large but faint. Its brightest star, Sadalsuud (Beta Aquarii), is magnitude 2.89, only slightly brighter than Sadalmelik (Alpha) at 2.94. The most recognisable pattern is the Water Jar, a small Y of four stars around Zeta Aquarii just south of the celestial equator. Look south of the Square of Pegasus and east of Capricornus to find it.

The Helix Nebula (NGC 7293, Caldwell 63) is a planetary nebula about 650 light-years away, one of the nearest of its kind. It is large but has a low surface brightness, and is best seen with binoculars or a wide-field telescope under dark skies. The globular cluster M2 is also within reach of binoculars. The Eta Aquariid meteor shower, debris from Halley's Comet, peaks in early May. Aquarius is best placed in the evening in October and is fully visible from between about 65° N and 86° S.

title: Aquila
subtitle: The Eagle

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: September (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Aquila is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. In Greek myth it is the eagle that carried Zeus's thunderbolts, and in some versions the bird that carried Ganymede up to Olympus, which links it to neighbouring Aquarius. The Milky Way runs through it, so binoculars show rich star fields.

Its brightest star, Altair (magnitude 0.76), is one of the nearest bright stars and one corner of the Summer Triangle, with Vega in Lyra and Deneb in Cygnus. Altair is easy to identify because it is flanked by two fainter stars, Tarazed and Alshain, which form a short line with it. The rest of the eagle's body and wings spreads south-west of this line toward the celestial equator.

Aquila straddles the celestial equator, so it can be seen from almost everywhere on Earth; it is fully visible from between about 78° N and 71° S. It is best placed in the evening in September. Eta Aquilae is one of the brightest Cepheid variable stars. It changes by almost a full magnitude over about a week, which can be followed with the naked eye by comparing it with nearby stars of known brightness.

title: Ara
subtitle: The Altar

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: July (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Ara is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. It represents the altar on which the Greek gods swore an oath of allegiance before their war against the Titans. The Milky Way above it was sometimes described as the smoke rising from the altar fire.

The constellation lies south of the tail of Scorpius, between Scorpius and Triangulum Australe. Its brightest star, Beta Arae, is an orange supergiant of magnitude 2.85, slightly brighter than Alpha Arae at 2.95. The main stars form a rough rectangle. Classical charts draw the altar with its flames pointing south, so to northern observers it appears upside down. Locate the curl of Scorpius's tail and the star Shaula, then look roughly 15 degrees further south.

Ara contains NGC 6397 (Caldwell 86), one of the nearest globular clusters to Earth at about 7,800 light-years. At magnitude 5.7 it is an easy binocular object. Hubble measured the cluster's distance directly by parallax and estimated its age at about 13.4 billion years. Ara is best placed in the evening in July and is fully visible from south of about 22° N; from mid-northern latitudes only its northern part rises.

title: Aries
subtitle: The Ram

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: December (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Aries is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations and a member of the zodiac. In Greek myth it is the ram with the golden fleece that rescued Phrixus and Helle, the fleece later sought by Jason and the Argonauts. About two thousand years ago the Sun stood in Aries at the March equinox, which is why that point is still called the First Point of Aries, even though precession has since carried it into Pisces.

The constellation is small and its main pattern is a short, bent line of three stars: Hamal (Alpha Arietis, magnitude 2.01), Sheratan and Mesarthim. Hamal is an orange giant and the only star in Aries brighter than magnitude 2.5. To find it, look between the Pleiades in Taurus and the Square of Pegasus, or follow a line south-east from Almach in Andromeda.

Mesarthim (Gamma Arietis) is a double star of two nearly equal white components that a small telescope separates easily. Aries has few bright deep-sky objects; its galaxies, such as NGC 772, need a moderate telescope. It is best placed in the evening in December and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 58° S.

title: Auriga
subtitle: The Charioteer

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: February (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Auriga is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. It is drawn as a charioteer holding a goat and her kids, and Greek writers most often identified him with Erichthonius, a legendary king of Athens credited with inventing the four-horse chariot. The bright star Capella takes its name from the Latin for "little she-goat", and the small triangle of faint stars just south of it are the Kids.

Capella (magnitude 0.08) is the brightest star in Auriga and one of the brightest in the night sky. It anchors a large pentagon of stars; the southernmost point of the pentagon is Elnath, which is formally assigned to Taurus. Capella lies north of Orion and Taurus, with the Pleiades to its south-west, and from mid-northern latitudes it passes nearly overhead on winter evenings.

The winter Milky Way runs through Auriga, and the open clusters M36, M37 and M38 lie in a line inside the pentagon, all within reach of binoculars. Epsilon Aurigae is an eclipsing binary in which a dark disk passes in front of the visible star every 27 years. The constellation is best placed in the evening in February and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 33° S.

title: Boötes
subtitle: The Herdsman

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: June (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Boötes is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. It is a herdsman or ploughman, usually pictured driving the bears Ursa Major and Ursa Minor around the pole; the name of its brightest star, Arcturus, means "guardian of the bear". In 1690 Hevelius added the hunting dogs of Canes Venatici at his side.

Arcturus, at magnitude −0.05, is the brightest star in the northern half of the celestial sphere and the fourth-brightest star in the night sky. It is an orange giant. The standard way to find it is to follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle away from the bowl, often remembered as "arc to Arcturus". The rest of Boötes forms a long kite shape extending north from Arcturus toward the Dipper's handle.

Izar (Epsilon Boötis) is a double star with a bright orange primary and a fainter bluish companion that needs a telescope at moderately high magnification. The Quadrantid meteor shower, which peaks in early January, radiates from the northern part of Boötes, in an area once occupied by the obsolete constellation Quadrans Muralis. Boötes is best placed in the evening in June and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 34° S.

title: Caelum
subtitle: The Engraving Tool

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: January (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Caelum is one of the fourteen constellations introduced by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille after his survey of the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope in 1751 and 1752. He called it les Burins, the engraver's chisels, rendered in Latin as Caela Sculptoris; the modern name is a shortened form. It has no mythology.

It is one of the smallest and faintest constellations, ranking 81st of 88 in area. Its brightest star, Alpha Caeli, is magnitude 4.45, and only a handful of its stars are brighter than fifth magnitude. Caelum lies in the space between Columba to the east and the winding line of Eridanus to the west, south of Lepus. The easiest approach is to find Phact, the brightest star of Columba, and look about 10 degrees to its west.

Caelum has no bright deep-sky objects; its galaxies require a telescope. It is best placed in the evening in January and is fully visible from south of about 41° N, so observers at mid-northern latitudes see it low in the south on winter evenings, if at all. Under dark southern skies it is a useful exercise in tracing faint stars.

title: Camelopardalis
subtitle: The Giraffe

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: February (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object
facts.value: NGC 2403 (Caldwell 7): spiral galaxy, 12 million light-years, magnitude 8.9

essay:
Camelopardalis was introduced by the Dutch astronomer Petrus Plancius, who drew it on a celestial globe in 1612; the German astronomer Jakob Bartsch included it in a star chart published in 1624. The name is the old Latin word for the giraffe, combining "camel" and "leopard". It fills a large region between the Pole Star and the bright constellations Auriga, Perseus and Cassiopeia that the Greeks left without a figure.

Camelopardalis ranks 18th of 88 in area but is faint. Its brightest star, Beta Camelopardalis, is only magnitude 4.02, and most of its stars are fourth or fifth magnitude, so it is hard to trace under city skies. It is easiest to locate by elimination: look in the empty-seeming region between Capella and Polaris.

Kemble's Cascade, a chain of about twenty faint stars ending at the small open cluster NGC 1502, is a well-known binocular sight here. The spiral galaxy NGC 2403 (Caldwell 7) lies about 12 million light-years away and at magnitude 8.9 can be seen in a small telescope. The constellation is circumpolar from latitudes north of about 37° N, stands highest in the evening in February, and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 3° S.

title: Cancer
subtitle: The Crab

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: March (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object
facts.value: M44, the Beehive Cluster (Praesepe): open cluster, 600 light-years, magnitude 3.7

essay:
Cancer is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations and a member of the zodiac. In Greek myth it is the crab that Hera sent to distract Heracles while he fought the Hydra; Heracles crushed it, and Hera placed it among the stars. The Tropic of Cancer is named after it because the Sun was in Cancer at the June solstice about two thousand years ago.

It is the faintest of the zodiac constellations. Its brightest star, Tarf (Beta Cancri), is magnitude 3.52. Cancer lies between Gemini and Leo: look roughly halfway between Pollux and Regulus. Under dark skies its main stars form an inverted Y.

The constellation's main attraction is the Beehive Cluster, M44, also called Praesepe. This open cluster is about 600 light-years away and has a combined magnitude of 3.7, so it is visible to the naked eye as a hazy patch and resolves into dozens of stars in binoculars. Galileo resolved it into individual stars with his first telescope in 1610. The smaller, fainter open cluster M67 lies near Alpha Cancri and is one of the oldest known open clusters. Cancer is best placed in the evening in March and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 56° S.

title: Canes Venatici
subtitle: The Hunting Dogs

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: May (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object
facts.value: M51, the Whirlpool Galaxy: spiral galaxy, 31 million light-years, magnitude 8.4

essay:
Canes Venatici was introduced by Johannes Hevelius and published in his star atlas Firmamentum Sobiescianum in 1690. The two hunting dogs are held on a leash by Boötes, the herdsman, as he follows the bears around the pole. Hevelius formed the figure from faint stars below the handle of the Big Dipper that Ptolemy had not assigned to any constellation.

The constellation has only one star brighter than fourth magnitude: Cor Caroli (Alpha-2 Canum Venaticorum), magnitude 2.88. Its name means "Charles's heart" and honours an English king Charles; sources differ on whether Charles I or Charles II was meant. Cor Caroli is a double star that small telescopes split easily. Find it below the curve of the Big Dipper's handle, roughly 15 to 20 degrees from it.

Canes Venatici lies well away from the Milky Way and contains many galaxies. The Whirlpool Galaxy, M51, is a face-on spiral about 31 million light-years away at magnitude 8.4; small telescopes show its smaller companion galaxy beside it. Other galaxies here include M94 and M106, and the bright globular cluster M3 lies near the border with Boötes. The constellation is best placed in the evening in May and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 37° S.

title: Canis Major
subtitle: The Great Dog

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: February (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Canis Major is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. It is the larger of Orion's two hunting dogs, following its master across the sky. Its main star, Sirius, was important to ancient Egyptian timekeeping, because its first appearance before sunrise each year came shortly before the annual Nile flood.

Sirius (Alpha Canis Majoris) is the brightest star in the night sky, at magnitude −1.46. It appears so bright mainly because it is close, at about 8.6 light-years. To find it, follow the three stars of Orion's Belt down and to the south-east. Several other bright stars outline the dog's body south of Sirius, including Adhara (Epsilon), Wezen (Delta) and Aludra (Eta). Sirius has a white dwarf companion, Sirius B, which is difficult to see in the glare of the primary.

The open cluster M41 lies about 4 degrees south of Sirius and is visible to the naked eye under dark skies; binoculars show dozens of its stars. Together with Procyon and Betelgeuse, Sirius forms the large Winter Triangle. Canis Major is best placed in the evening in February and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 56° N.

title: Canis Minor
subtitle: The Lesser Dog

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: March (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Canis Minor is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. It is the smaller of Orion's two hunting dogs. The name of its brightest star, Procyon, means "before the dog" in Greek, because from Mediterranean latitudes it rises shortly before Sirius, the Dog Star.

Procyon (magnitude 0.37) is one of the brightest stars in the sky and one of the nearest, at about 11.5 light-years. Like Sirius, it has a faint white dwarf companion. The only other prominent star in the constellation is Gomeisa (Beta Canis Minoris), so the figure is just a short line of two stars. Find Procyon east of Betelgeuse in Orion; with Betelgeuse and Sirius it forms the large Winter Triangle.

The constellation is small, ranking 71st of 88 in area, and contains no bright deep-sky objects. It lies just north of the celestial equator, so it can be seen from almost every inhabited place on Earth; it is fully visible from between about 89° N and 76° S. It is best placed in the evening in March, when it stands high in the south for northern observers and high in the north for southern ones.

title: Capricornus
subtitle: The Sea Goat

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: September (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Capricornus is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations and part of the zodiac. Its sea-goat figure, with the head and forelegs of a goat and the tail of a fish, goes back to Babylonian astronomy. Greek writers linked it to the god Pan, who was said to have jumped into the Nile and taken this shape while escaping the monster Typhon. The Tropic of Capricorn takes its name from the constellation, which held the December solstice in antiquity.

The stars are faint and form a broad triangle or boat shape. The brightest is Deneb Algedi (Delta Capricorni) at magnitude 2.83, an eclipsing binary at the eastern end. At the western tip, Algedi (Alpha Capricorni) is a naked-eye double: two unrelated stars that happen to lie in nearly the same direction. A line from Vega through Altair, continued southward, reaches the western end of Capricornus.

The globular cluster M30 lies about 28,000 light-years away and is magnitude 7.7, a modest binocular or small-telescope object near the eastern end of the figure. Capricornus is best placed in the evening in September and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 62° N.

title: Carina
subtitle: The Ship's Keel

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: March (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object
facts.value: Carina Nebula (NGC 3372, Caldwell 92): emission nebula, 7,500 light-years, magnitude 4.8

essay:
Carina was once part of Argo Navis, the ship of Jason and the Argonauts, which Ptolemy listed as one of his 48 constellations. Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille divided the large ship into Carina (the keel), Puppis (the stern) and Vela (the sails) in the 1750s. Because the stars kept the Greek letters assigned across the whole ship, Carina has an Alpha and a Beta but no Gamma or Delta, which are in Vela.

Canopus, Alpha Carinae, is the second-brightest star in the night sky at magnitude −0.74. It is a bright giant far more luminous than Sirius, and spacecraft have used it as a reference star for orientation. With two stars of Vela, Carina also forms the False Cross, which is sometimes mistaken for the Southern Cross.

The Carina Nebula (NGC 3372, Caldwell 92) is an emission nebula about 7,500 light-years away and magnitude 4.8, visible to the naked eye as a bright patch in the southern Milky Way. It contains Eta Carinae, a massive, unstable binary star system that had a great eruption in the 1840s. Lacaille discovered the nebula from the Cape of Good Hope in 1752. Carina is best placed in the evening in March and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 14° N.

title: Cassiopeia
subtitle: The Queen

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: November (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Cassiopeia is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. In Greek myth she was the queen of Ethiopia, wife of Cepheus and mother of Andromeda, whose boast about beauty provoked Poseidon to send the sea monster Cetus. She was placed in the sky on a throne that circles the pole, so she spends part of each night upside down.

Its five main stars form a W or M shape that is easy to recognise. The brightest is Schedar (Alpha Cassiopeiae) at magnitude 2.23, only just ahead of Caph (Beta) at 2.27. Gamma Cassiopeiae, at the centre of the W, is an irregular variable star. Cassiopeia lies on the opposite side of Polaris from the Big Dipper, so when one is low the other is high.

The Milky Way runs through Cassiopeia and it is rich in open clusters, including M52 and M103, both visible in binoculars. In 1572 Tycho Brahe observed a supernova here, now known as Tycho's Supernova; its remnant is a radio and X-ray source. Cassiopeia is circumpolar from latitudes north of about 43° N. essay:
Centaurus is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations and the ninth-largest of the 88. It represents a centaur, usually identified with Chiron, the teacher of heroes such as Achilles and Jason. In Ptolemy's time it also included the stars now assigned to Crux.

Its brightest star, Alpha Centauri, is the nearest star system to the Sun. To the eye it is a single point, but a small telescope splits it into Rigil Kentaurus (Alpha Centauri A, magnitude 0.01) and Toliman (Alpha Centauri B, magnitude 1.33). A third, faint member, Proxima Centauri, is the nearest known star to the Sun. Hadar (Beta Centauri, magnitude 0.58) lies close by, and the two form the Pointers, which lead to the Southern Cross.

Omega Centauri (NGC 5139, Caldwell 80) is the largest and brightest globular cluster in the sky, about 17,000 light-years away and magnitude 3.7, with about 10 million stars. Ptolemy catalogued it as a single star. Centaurus A (Caldwell 77), about 11 million light-years away, is the closest active galaxy to Earth and shows in small telescopes as a glow crossed by a dark dust lane. Centaurus is best placed in the evening in May and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 25° N.

title: Cepheus
subtitle: The King

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: October (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object
facts.value: NGC 6946 (Caldwell 12), on the border with Cygnus: spiral galaxy, 15 million light-years, magnitude 9.7

essay:
Cepheus is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. In Greek myth he was king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda. His figure lies next to his queen near the north celestial pole.

The main stars form a shape like a simple house with a pointed roof, the roof pointing toward Polaris. The brightest is Alderamin (Alpha Cephei) at magnitude 2.46. Because of precession, the north celestial pole is moving through Cepheus, and in several thousand years Gamma and later Alpha Cephei will be the nearest bright stars to the pole. To find Cepheus, look between the W of Cassiopeia and the head of Draco.

Delta Cephei, near the south-eastern corner of the house, is the prototype of the Cepheid variables, stars whose pulsation period is linked to their luminosity, which made them a key tool for measuring distances to other galaxies. Mu Cephei, Herschel's Garnet Star, is one of the reddest stars visible to the naked eye. The spiral galaxy NGC 6946 (Caldwell 12), on the border with Cygnus, has had ten observed supernovae since 1917. Cepheus is circumpolar from latitudes north of about 37° N, best placed in the evening in October, and fully visible from anywhere north of about 1° S.

title: Cetus

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: December (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object
facts.value: M77: spiral galaxy with an active nucleus, 45 million light-years, magnitude 9.6

essay:
Cetus is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations and the fourth-largest of the 88. It represents the sea monster sent by Poseidon to ravage the coast of Ethiopia after Queen Cassiopeia's boast, the creature from which Perseus rescued Andromeda.

Although large, Cetus has few bright stars. The brightest is Diphda (Beta Ceti, magnitude 2.01), in the tail, which stands alone in a sparse area south of the Square of Pegasus. Menkar (Alpha Ceti, 2.53) marks the head, south of Aries and south-west of the Pleiades. Between them lies Mira (Omicron Ceti), the first star of its kind recognised as variable, after David Fabricius noticed it in 1596. Mira swings from about third magnitude to well below naked-eye visibility over roughly 11 months.

The spiral galaxy M77, about 45 million light-years away and magnitude 9.6, has an unusually bright, active core and is one of the prototypes of the Seyfert galaxies. Tau Ceti, a Sun-like star about 12 light-years away, is one of the nearest single stars visible without a telescope. Cetus is best placed in the evening in December and is fully visible from between about 65° N and 79° S.

title: Chamaeleon
subtitle: The Chameleon

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: April (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Chamaeleon is one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius from observations made by the Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman in the 1590s. It first appeared on a celestial globe in 1598 and in Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603. The figure is the lizard known for changing colour.

It is a small, faint constellation close to the south celestial pole. The brightest star, Alpha Chamaeleontis, is magnitude 4.05, and the main stars form a small elongated diamond. To locate it, find the Southern Cross and follow its long axis toward the pole for about 20 degrees. From southern temperate latitudes Chamaeleon is circumpolar and can be seen on any clear night.

Chamaeleon contains a group of dark molecular clouds, the Chamaeleon complex, which is one of the nearest regions of active star formation to the Sun. Its young stars are hidden by dust at visible wavelengths and are studied mainly with infrared telescopes. The small planetary nebula NGC 3195 is a target for telescopes of moderate size. Chamaeleon is best placed in the evening around April and is fully visible only from south of about 6° N, so it is out of reach for nearly all northern observers.

title: Circinus
subtitle: The Drawing Compass

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: June (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Circinus is one of the fourteen constellations introduced by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 1750s after his survey of the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope. It represents a pair of drawing compasses, one of several surveying and drafting instruments he placed in this part of the sky alongside Norma, the set square.

Circinus is the fourth-smallest constellation, ranking 85th of 88 in area. Its brightest star, Alpha Circini, is magnitude 3.19. It is the brightest of the rapidly oscillating Ap stars, which show tiny brightness changes over a few minutes. The easiest way to find Circinus is from Alpha Centauri: the constellation lies just to its east, between Alpha Centauri and Triangulum Australe.

The Milky Way passes through Circinus, giving rich star fields in binoculars. The Circinus Galaxy, a nearby active galaxy hidden behind the dust of the Milky Way, was only identified in the 1970s and is a target for professional instruments rather than visual observers. Circinus is best placed in the evening around June and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 19° N. From mid-northern latitudes it never rises.

title: Columba
subtitle: The Dove

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: February (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Columba was introduced by the Dutch astronomer Petrus Plancius, who drew it on a map in 1592 as Noah's dove, the bird sent from the ark to look for dry land. It was formed from stars south of Lepus that Ptolemy had not included in any figure, and Augustin Royer included it in his star atlas of 1679.

The brightest star is Phact (Alpha Columbae), magnitude 2.65. With Wazn (Beta Columbae) it forms a short line marking the dove's body. To find Columba, look south of Lepus, which lies directly below Orion's feet, and south-west of Sirius in Canis Major.

Mu Columbae is a runaway star. It and AE Aurigae are moving rapidly away from the region of Orion in opposite directions, and their paths trace back to a common origin about 2.5 million years ago, probably the break-up of a multiple star system. The globular cluster NGC 1851 is a compact target for small telescopes. Columba is best placed in the evening in February and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 46° N, so northern observers see it low in the south on winter evenings.

title: Coma Berenices

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: May (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object

essay:
Coma Berenices recalls Queen Berenice II of Egypt, who is said to have cut off her hair as an offering for the safe return of her husband, Ptolemy III, from war. When the hair disappeared from the temple, the court astronomer Conon of Samos announced that it had been placed among the stars. Ptolemy treated these stars as an asterism attached to Leo; Gerardus Mercator showed them as a separate constellation on his celestial globe of 1551, and Tycho Brahe included it in his star catalogue of 1602.

The constellation is faint. Its brightest star, Beta Comae Berenices, is only magnitude 4.25. Its most visible feature is the Coma Star Cluster (Melotte 111), a loose group of fifth- and sixth-magnitude stars spread over several degrees and best seen in binoculars. Find it between Denebola, the tail of Leo, and Arcturus.

The north galactic pole lies in Coma Berenices, so the view here is out of the plane of the Milky Way and many distant galaxies are visible. The Black Eye Galaxy, M64, about 17 million light-years away and magnitude 9.8, has a dark band of dust across its core. The constellation also contains the Coma Cluster of galaxies. It is best placed in the evening in May and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 56° S.

title: Corona Australis
subtitle: The Southern Crown

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: August (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Corona Australis is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. It is a curved line of faint stars that the Greeks saw as a wreath or crown, sometimes said to have fallen from the head of Sagittarius, beside whose feet it lies.

The constellation is small, ranking 80th of 88 in area, and its two brightest stars are nearly equal: Meridiana (Alpha Coronae Australis) at magnitude 4.09 and Beta at 4.10. The arc of stars is distinctive under dark skies. Find it just south of the Teapot asterism of Sagittarius, east of the stinger at the end of Scorpius's tail.

The Milky Way runs along the edge of Corona Australis. The Corona Australis molecular cloud, near the star R Coronae Australis, is one of the nearest star-forming regions to the Sun and appears in photographs as a mix of dark dust and blue reflection nebulae. The globular cluster NGC 6541 (Caldwell 78) is about 22,000 light-years away and magnitude 6.3, within reach of binoculars. Corona Australis is best placed in the evening in August and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 44° N; from mid-northern latitudes it stays low on the southern horizon in summer.

facts.label: Best evening visibility

essay:
Corona Borealis is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. In Greek myth it is the crown given by Dionysus to Ariadne, the Cretan princess who helped Theseus escape the Labyrinth; Dionysus later set it in the sky.

It is a small semicircle of seven stars, compact and easy to recognise. The brightest is Alphecca (Alpha Coronae Borealis), magnitude 2.24, which sits in the middle of the arc like the jewel of the crown. Find the Northern Crown about a third of the way from Arcturus toward Vega, just east of the kite of Boötes.

Two well-known variable stars lie here. R Coronae Borealis is the prototype of a class of stars that fade by several magnitudes for months at a time when clouds of carbon dust form around them. T Coronae Borealis is a recurrent nova: normally about tenth magnitude, it has brightened to naked-eye visibility in recorded outbursts, including those of 1866 and 1946. The constellation lies away from the Milky Way and contains the Corona Borealis Galaxy Cluster, which is too faint for small telescopes. It is best placed in the evening in July and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 50° S.

Corvus is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. In Greek myth Apollo sent a crow to fetch water in a cup; the bird delayed, then blamed a water snake for its lateness. Apollo saw through the lie and set the crow, the cup (Crater) and the snake (Hydra) in the sky, with the crow kept just out of reach of the cup.

The main stars form a compact quadrilateral, sometimes called the Sail, which is easy to see despite its modest brightness. The brightest is Gienah (Gamma Corvi) at magnitude 2.58. Alpha Corvi, named Alchiba, is fainter than all four corner stars. Find Corvus about 15 degrees south-west of Spica in Virgo.

The Antennae Galaxies (NGC 4038 and 4039, Caldwell 60 and 61) are a pair of colliding spiral galaxies about 65 million light-years away. Their long tidal tails, made of stars pulled out during the encounter, give them their name. At magnitudes 10.5 and 11.0 they need a telescope of moderate size. The pair has been interacting for a few hundred million years. Corvus is best placed in the evening in May and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 64° N.

title: Crater
subtitle: The Cup

facts.label: Best evening visibility

essay:
Crater is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. It is the cup of Apollo in the same myth as neighbouring Corvus: the crow, sent with the cup to fetch water, was punished for its delay and its lie, and the cup was placed in the sky just beyond the crow's reach, on the back of Hydra.

Crater is faint, with no star brighter than third magnitude. Its brightest star is Delta Crateris, an orange giant of magnitude 3.56; Alpha Crateris, named Alkes, is fainter. The main stars form a goblet shape. Find Crater immediately west of the Corvus quadrilateral, south of the hindquarters of Leo and above the long body of Hydra.

Crater lies far from the Milky Way and contains only faint galaxies. The Crater 2 dwarf galaxy, a satellite of the Milky Way identified in 2016 from survey data, is one of the largest and most diffuse satellites known, but it cannot be seen in amateur telescopes. Crater is best placed in the evening in April and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 64° N. essay:
Crux is the smallest of the 88 constellations. Ptolemy listed its stars as part of Centaurus, and European navigators sailing south in the 16th century began treating the cross as a separate figure. It appeared on Dutch celestial globes around the end of that century and was established as a constellation in Augustin Royer's star atlas of 1679.

Four bright stars form the cross. Acrux (Alpha Crucis), at the foot, is a double star whose two components are magnitude 1.28 and 1.58; together they outshine Mimosa (Beta Crucis), the brightest single star at 1.25. The long axis of the cross, from Gacrux through Acrux, points toward the south celestial pole, which made Crux a traditional aid to navigation. The two Pointers, Alpha and Beta Centauri, lie to its east and distinguish it from the larger, fainter False Cross in Carina and Vela.

Next to Mimosa is the Jewel Box (NGC 4755, Caldwell 94), an open cluster about 6,500 light-years away and magnitude 4.2, about 16 million years old. Beside the cross lies the Coalsack (Caldwell 99), a dark nebula about 600 light-years away that blocks the Milky Way behind it and is plain to the naked eye. Crux is best placed in the evening in May and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 25° N.

title: Cygnus
subtitle: The Swan

facts.label: Best evening visibility

facts.value: North America Nebula (NGC 7000, Caldwell 20): emission nebula, 1,800 light-years, magnitude 5.0

essay:
Cygnus is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. Greek myth offers several swans, the best known being the form Zeus took to visit Leda. The figure flies south along the Milky Way with its long neck stretched toward Sagittarius, and its brightest stars form the Northern Cross.

Deneb (Alpha Cygni, magnitude 1.25) marks the swan's tail and the top of the cross. It is a white supergiant, one of the most luminous stars visible to the eye, and one corner of the Summer Triangle with Vega and Altair. At the other end of the cross, Albireo (Beta Cygni) marks the swan's head; a small telescope shows it as a golden star and a blue one.

The Milky Way is bright here and is split by the Great Rift, a lane of dust. The North America Nebula (NGC 7000, Caldwell 20), about 1,800 light-years away and magnitude 5.0, lies near Deneb and shows in binoculars under dark skies. The Veil Nebula is the remnant of an ancient supernova. 61 Cygni was the first star to have its distance measured by parallax, by Friedrich Bessel in 1838, and Cygnus X-1 was the first X-ray source widely accepted as a black hole. Cygnus is best placed in the evening in September and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 28° S.

Its name refers to the dolphinfish, or mahi-mahi, which the sailors would have seen in tropical waters; it is sometimes drawn as a swordfish.

The stars are faint. The brightest, Alpha Doradus, is magnitude 3.28. Dorado lies between Canopus and the south celestial pole, and most of the Large Magellanic Cloud falls inside its boundaries. The Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, appears to the naked eye as a detached patch of the Milky Way and is the simplest way to locate the constellation.

Inside the Large Magellanic Cloud is the Tarantula Nebula (30 Doradus, Caldwell 103), about 170,000 light-years away and magnitude 4.0. It is the most productive star-forming region in the nearby universe and home to the most massive stars known. In 1987 the supernova SN 1987A, the nearest seen since 1604, appeared in the Large Magellanic Cloud close to the Tarantula. Dorado is best placed in the evening in January and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 19° N.

The dragon's body winds between Ursa Major and Ursa Minor, and its head is a quadrilateral of four stars close to Vega. The brightest star, Eltanin (Gamma Draconis, magnitude 2.23), is in the head. Thuban (Alpha Draconis), much fainter, lies between Mizar in the Big Dipper's handle and Kochab in the Little Dipper. The Draconid meteor shower in early October radiates from the dragon's head. Draco is circumpolar from latitudes north of about 42° N, best placed in the evening in July, and fully visible from anywhere north of about 3° S.

title: Equuleus
subtitle: The Little Horse

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: September (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Equuleus is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations and the second-smallest of the 88, ranking 87th in area. It represents the head of a small horse or foal, sometimes said to be Celeris, the brother of Pegasus. It may have been introduced by the Greek astronomer Hipparchus, whose work Ptolemy drew on.

The constellation is faint, with no star brighter than fourth magnitude. The brightest, Kitalpha (Alpha Equulei), is magnitude 3.93; its name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning "part of the horse". The main stars form a small, irregular quadrilateral. Find Equuleus between the diamond of Delphinus and Enif, the bright star at the nose of Pegasus.

Equuleus has no bright deep-sky objects, though it contains several double stars. Delta Equulei is a close binary with an orbital period of about 5.7 years, one of the shortest among binaries whose stars can be resolved by telescope. The constellation lies just north of the celestial equator, so it is visible from nearly all of the inhabited Earth. It is best placed in the evening in September and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 76° S.

title: Eridanus
subtitle: The River

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: January (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Eridanus is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations and the sixth-largest of the 88. It represents a river, identified in Greek myth with the Po of northern Italy, into which Phaethon fell after losing control of the chariot of the Sun. Ptolemy's river ended at the star now called Acamar (Theta Eridani); later astronomers extended it south to Achernar, a star that does not rise from Greece.

The river begins near Rigel in Orion, at Cursa (Beta Eridani), and winds west and then south across nearly 60 degrees of declination. Its brightest star, Achernar (Alpha Eridani, magnitude 0.46), marks the southern end; the name means "end of the river". Achernar is one of the fastest-rotating stars known and is noticeably flattened.

Epsilon Eridani, about 10.5 light-years away, is one of the nearest Sun-like stars and is surrounded by a disk of debris. The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1300 is a well-known target for astrophotographers. Because it spans so wide a range of declination, Eridanus can be seen in full only from latitudes between about 32° N and 89° S. It is best placed in the evening in January; mid-northern observers see only its upper reaches.

title: Fornax
subtitle: The Furnace

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: December (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object
facts.value: Hubble Ultra Deep Field: a small patch of Fornax containing about 10,000 galaxies

essay:
Fornax is one of the fourteen constellations introduced by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 1750s after his survey of the southern sky. He named it the chemical furnace, Fornax Chemica, after an apparatus used in laboratory chemistry, and the name was later shortened. It has no mythology.

The constellation is faint. Its brightest star, Dalim (Alpha Fornacis), is magnitude 3.98. Fornax lies inside the large westward loop of Eridanus, south of Cetus; the practical way to find it is to trace Eridanus from Rigel and look in the area the river encloses.

Fornax lies far from the Milky Way and contains the Fornax Cluster, one of the nearest clusters of galaxies, whose members include the barred spiral NGC 1365 and the radio galaxy Fornax A. The Fornax Dwarf, a faint satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, also lies here. The Hubble Ultra Deep Field, which shows about 10,000 galaxies, some seen as they were within a few hundred million years of the big bang, was taken in a small patch of Fornax chosen because it has few bright foreground stars. Fornax is best placed in the evening in December and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 50° N.

title: Gemini
subtitle: The Twins

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: February (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Gemini is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations and part of the zodiac. Its two brightest stars are named for the twins Castor and Pollux, brothers of Helen of Troy, who sailed with the Argonauts and were regarded as protectors of sailors. When Castor, the mortal twin, was killed, Pollux asked to share his immortality with him, and Zeus placed both in the sky.

Pollux (Beta Geminorum, magnitude 1.14) is the brighter of the pair, an orange giant with a known planet. Castor (Alpha) is slightly fainter. A small telescope splits it into two close stars, and each of those, together with a faint third component, is itself a binary, making six stars in all. The twins' bodies form two roughly parallel lines of stars extending south-west toward Orion. A line from Rigel through Betelgeuse leads to Gemini.

The open cluster M35, about 2,800 light-years away and magnitude 5.3, lies near the feet of the twins and shows in binoculars. The Eskimo Nebula, NGC 2392, is a planetary nebula for small telescopes. The Geminid meteor shower, one of the strongest of the year, peaks in mid-December with its radiant near Castor. Gemini is best placed in the evening in February and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 54° S.

title: Grus
subtitle: The Crane

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: October (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Grus is one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius from observations made by the Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman in the 1590s. It first appeared on a globe in 1598 and in Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603. It represents a crane. Some of its stars had earlier been counted by Arab astronomers as part of the Southern Fish, Piscis Austrinus.

The brightest star is Alnair (Alpha Gruis), a blue-white star of magnitude 1.71. Beta Gruis, a red giant of similar brightness, lies close by, and the colour contrast between the two is easy to see with the naked eye. A line of stars runs north-west from the body to Gamma Gruis, marking the crane's neck. Find Grus south-west of Fomalhaut, the bright star of Piscis Austrinus.

Delta and Mu Gruis are wide naked-eye pairs, each made of two stars that lie in nearly the same direction but at different distances. The constellation contains several galaxies visible in larger telescopes, including the Grus Quartet, a group of interacting spirals. Grus is best placed in the evening in October and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 33° N.

title: Hercules
subtitle: Hercules

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: July (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object
facts.value: M13, the Great Globular Cluster: 25,000 light-years, magnitude 5.8

essay:
Hercules is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations and the fifth-largest of the 88. Ptolemy knew it as the Kneeler, an unnamed figure kneeling with one foot on the head of Draco; later writers identified him with Heracles, the hero of the twelve labours. For northern observers the figure appears upside down.

Hercules has no first-magnitude star. Its brightest, Kornephoros (Beta Herculis), is magnitude 2.77. The most recognisable pattern is the Keystone, a quadrilateral of four third-magnitude stars marking the hero's torso. Find it about a third of the way from Vega to Arcturus. Rasalgethi (Alpha Herculis), at the hero's head near Ophiuchus, is a red giant that varies irregularly in brightness.

On the western side of the Keystone is M13, the Great Globular Cluster, about 25,000 light-years away and magnitude 5.8. Edmond Halley discovered it in 1714. It is visible in binoculars as a fuzzy star and resolves into stars in a moderate telescope. A second globular cluster, M92, lies north of the Keystone and is often overlooked because of its neighbour. Hercules is best placed in the evening in July and is fully visible from anywhere north of about 38° S.

title: Horologium
subtitle: The Pendulum Clock

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: December (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Horologium is one of the fourteen constellations introduced by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 1750s, after his survey of the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope. It represents a pendulum clock, an instrument then essential for timing astronomical observations. It has no mythology.

The constellation is long and faint, running north to south beside the lower course of Eridanus. Its brightest star, Alpha Horologii, is an orange giant of magnitude 3.86, and most of the rest are fifth magnitude. Find it east of Achernar and west of the Large Magellanic Cloud, with Reticulum on its eastern side.

The globular cluster NGC 1261 (Caldwell 87) lies about 50,000 light-years away and is magnitude 8.3, a target for small telescopes. Horologium also contains the Horologium Supercluster, a large concentration of galaxy clusters that is far too faint to see but is prominent in maps of the large-scale structure of the universe. Horologium is best placed in the evening in December and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 22° N. From southern temperate latitudes it is well placed through the summer months, December to February.

title: Hydra
subtitle: The Water Snake

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: April (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

facts.label: Notable deep-sky object
facts.value: M83, the Southern Pinwheel: spiral galaxy, 15 million light-years, magnitude 7.5

essay:
Hydra is the largest of the 88 constellations and one of Ptolemy's 48. In Greek myth it is identified with the many-headed Lernaean Hydra killed by Heracles, and also with the water snake in the story of Corvus and Crater, which ride on its back.

Hydra stretches across almost seven hours of right ascension, from south of Cancer to south of Libra. Its head, a small group of stars just south of Cancer and east of Procyon, is the best place to start. The brightest star, Alphard (Alpha Hydrae, magnitude 1.97), lies alone in a sparse region; its name means "the solitary one". From Alphard the body runs south-east beneath Crater and Corvus toward Centaurus.

The spiral galaxy M83, the Southern Pinwheel, is about 15 million light-years away and magnitude 7.5, one of the brightest spiral galaxies in the sky. Hydra also contains the open cluster M48, the globular cluster M68 and the planetary nebula NGC 3242, known as the Ghost of Jupiter. Hydra is best placed in the evening in April and is fully visible from between about 54° N and 83° S.

title: Hydrus
subtitle: The Lesser Water Snake

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: December (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Hydrus is one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius from observations made by the Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman in the 1590s. It first appeared on a globe in 1598 and in Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603. It represents a lesser water snake, distinct from the much larger Hydra.

Hydrus lies close to the south celestial pole, between the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. Its three brightest stars form a large triangle. The brightest, Beta Hydri (magnitude 2.79), is the nearest bright star to the south celestial pole; it is a Sun-like star about 24 light-years away and older than the Sun. Alpha Hydri (2.84) lies about 5 degrees from Achernar, which makes a convenient starting point: from Achernar look south for Alpha Hydri, then follow the triangle toward the pole.

Hydrus lies far from the plane of the Milky Way and has few bright deep-sky objects; its galaxies need a telescope. From southern temperate latitudes it is circumpolar and visible on any clear night. It is best placed in the evening in December and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 7° N, so it is out of reach for nearly all northern observers.

title: Indus
subtitle: The Indian

facts.label: Best evening visibility
facts.value: October (on the meridian around 21:00 local time)

essay:
Indus is one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius from observations made by the Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman in the 1590s. It first appeared on a globe in 1598 and in Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603. It depicts an indigenous man holding arrows; which people the figure was meant to represent is not recorded.

The constellation is faint. Its brightest star, Alpha Indi, is an orange giant of magnitude 3.11. Indus is bordered by Pavo to the west, Grus and Tucana to the east, and Microscopium and Sagittarius to the north. A practical way to find it is to locate Peacock, the bright star of Pavo, and look about 10 degrees north for Alpha Indi.

Epsilon Indi is one of the nearest stars to the Sun, at about 12 light-years. It has a pair of brown dwarf companions and a giant planet, and it is just visible to the naked eye from a dark site. The constellation contains several galaxies for larger telescopes. Indus is best placed in the evening in October and is fully visible from anywhere south of about 15° N.
